Notation and conventions

Matthew Litwin 2026-06-23

The index, sign and typeface conventions of this book, and a table of its symbols. Where standard texts disagree, the choice made here is stated with its source.

Indices

Indices Range Used for
i,j,k,ℓi, j, k, \elli,j,k,ℓ 1,…,n1, \ldots, n1,…,n coordinate indices on a general manifold (Part I) and on a configuration space QQQ
μ,ν,ρ,σ,λ\mu, \nu, \rho, \sigma, \lambdaμ,ν,ρ,σ,λ (mu, nu, rho, sigma, lambda) 1,…,n1, \ldots, n1,…,n; 0,…,30, \ldots, 30,…,3 on spacetime tensor components from chapter 4 on
i,j,ki, j, ki,j,k in a spacetime context 1,2,31, 2, 31,2,3 spatial components
A,BA, BA,B 1,…,N1, \ldots, N1,…,N particle labels: rA\tens{r}_ArA​, mAm_AmA​, ∑A\sum_A∑A​
a,ba, ba,b 0,…,30, \ldots, 30,…,3 orthonormal-frame (tetrad) indices, Cartan formalism only
  • Position. An upper index marks a TpMT_p MTp​M slot (contravariant), a lower index a Tp∗MT^*_p MTp∗​M slot (covariant). Coordinates carry upper indices, xμx^\muxμ. Momenta carry lower ones, pip_ipi​.
  • . An index appearing once up and once down in a term is summed over its range. Pairs in the same position are never summed.
  • Coordinate names as indices. A coordinate’s name may replace its index value: gθφg_{\theta\varphi}gθφ​, Γθφφ\Gamma^\theta{}_{\varphi\varphi}Γθφφ​.
  • Marks. A prime or tilde marks a second chart: x′μ′x'^{\mu'}x′μ′, θ~\tilde\thetaθ~. Brackets denote symmetrization and antisymmetrization, T(μν)T_{(\mu\nu)}T(μν)​ and T[μν]T_{[\mu\nu]}T[μν]​, with weight 1/k!1/k!1/k!.

Einstein’s 1916 paper, where the summation convention was introduced, used Greek indices running 111 to 444, wrote coordinates with lower indices xνx_\nuxν​, and put time last. The other choices here follow Misner–Thorne–Wheeler (MTW) and Carroll.

Einstein summation

The convention, due to Einstein and assumed tacitly wherever it is in force: a Greek (or Latin) index appearing exactly once up and exactly once down in the same monomial is summed over its range. So

vμωμ:=∑μvμωμ,Tμν Sνρ:=∑νTμν Sνρ.v^\mu \omega_\mu := \sum_{\mu} v^\mu \omega_\mu, \qquad T^\mu{}_\nu\, S^\nu{}_\rho := \sum_{\nu} T^\mu{}_\nu\, S^\nu{}_\rho. vμωμ​:=μ∑​vμωμ​,Tμν​Sνρ​:=ν∑​Tμν​Sνρ​.

Two ramifications. First, repeated indices in the same vertical position (vμωμv^\mu \omega^\muvμωμ, TμμT_{\mu\mu}Tμμ​) are almost always an error — there is no canonical pairing without a metric. Second, an index used as a dummy variable is bound and can be renamed: vμωμ=vνωνv^\mu \omega_\mu = v^\nu \omega_\nuvμωμ​=vνων​. Be wary of dummy collisions when chaining contractions.

Riemann tensor

The (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3)-tensor R(X,Y)Z=∇X∇YZ−∇Y∇XZ−∇[X,Y]Z\tens{R}(\tens{X}, \tens{Y}) \tens{Z} = \nabla_{\tens{X}} \nabla_{\tens{Y}} \tens{Z} - \nabla_{\tens{Y}} \nabla_{\tens{X}} \tens{Z} - \nabla_{[\tens{X}, \tens{Y}]} \tens{Z}R(X,Y)Z=∇X​∇Y​Z−∇Y​∇X​Z−∇[X,Y]​Z, with components RρσμνR^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}Rρσμν​ in the book’s . It measures the failure of around a small loop to return a vector to itself. For the Levi-Civita connection the lowered tensor RρσμνR_{\rho\sigma\mu\nu}Rρσμν​ has these symmetries:

  • antisymmetric in each pair;
  • symmetric under exchange of the pairs;
  • satisfies the first Bianchi identity.

That leaves n2(n2−1)/12n^2(n^2 - 1)/12n2(n2−1)/12 independent components, 20 in four dimensions. Defined on the torsion-and-curvature page.

Riemann index convention

This book (following Misner–Thorne–Wheeler and Carroll) writes

Rρσμν=∂μΓρνσ−∂νΓρμσ+Γρμλ Γλνσ−Γρνλ Γλμσ,R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu \Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu \Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma} + \Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\lambda}\, \Gamma^\lambda{}_{\nu\sigma} - \Gamma^\rho{}_{\nu\lambda}\, \Gamma^\lambda{}_{\mu\sigma}, Rρσμν​=∂μ​Γρνσ​−∂ν​Γρμσ​+Γρμλ​Γλνσ​−Γρνλ​Γλμσ​,

matching R(X,Y)Z:=∇X∇YZ−∇Y∇XZ−∇[X,Y]Z\tens{R}(\tens{X}, \tens{Y}) \tens{Z} := \nabla_{\tens{X}} \nabla_{\tens{Y}} \tens{Z} - \nabla_{\tens{Y}} \nabla_{\tens{X}} \tens{Z} - \nabla_{[\tens{X}, \tens{Y}]} \tens{Z}R(X,Y)Z:=∇X​∇Y​Z−∇Y​∇X​Z−∇[X,Y]​Z: the output index ρ\rhoρ first, then the index σ\sigmaσ of the vector being transported, then the two antisymmetrized loop directions μ,ν\mu, \nuμ,ν. Mnemonic: of Z\tens{Z}Z around the small loop with sides εu,εv\varepsilon \tens{u}, \varepsilon \tens{v}εu,εv (u\tens{u}u first) changes it by −ε2R(u,v) Z-\varepsilon^2 \tens{R}(\tens{u}, \tens{v})\, \tens{Z}−ε2R(u,v)Z. Other texts permute slots or flip the overall sign — check conventions before comparing formulas.

Wedge convention

This book writes a kkk-form in the 1/k!1/k!1/k! convention:

ω=1k! ωμ1⋯μk dxμ1∧⋯∧dxμk,\tens{\omega} = \frac{1}{k!}\, \omega_{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}\, dx^{\mu_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^{\mu_k}, ω=k!1​ωμ1​⋯μk​​dxμ1​∧⋯∧dxμk​,

with ωμ1⋯μk\omega_{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}ωμ1​⋯μk​​ totally antisymmetric and the sum over all index tuples. The common alternative — the strictly-increasing-index convention —

ω=∑μ1<⋯<μkωμ1⋯μk dxμ1∧⋯∧dxμk\tens{\omega} = \sum_{\mu_1 < \cdots < \mu_k} \omega_{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}\, dx^{\mu_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^{\mu_k} ω=μ1​<⋯<μk​∑​ωμ1​⋯μk​​dxμ1​∧⋯∧dxμk​

carries no combinatorial prefactor and sums only over ordered tuples. The two give the same component array on ordered tuples (e.g. ωθφ=sin⁡θ\omega_{\theta\varphi} = \sin\thetaωθφ​=sinθ for the sphere’s area form either way); they differ only in whether the basis is reduced to ordered tuples or the components are antisymmetrized and divided by k!k!k!. Watch for the factor when comparing formulas across textbooks.

Poisson bracket

{f,g}=∂f∂qi∂g∂pi−∂f∂pi∂g∂qi=Xg(f),\{f, g\} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q^i} = \tens{X}_g(f), {f,g}=∂qi∂f​∂pi​∂g​−∂pi​∂f​∂qi∂g​=Xg​(f),

with {qi,pj}=δji\{q^i, p_j\} = \delta^i_j{qi,pj​}=δji​. It is antisymmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity, and is a derivation in each slot. Time evolution is f˙={f,H}+∂tf\dot f = \{f, H\} + \partial_t ff˙​={f,H}+∂t​f, so fff is conserved iff {f,H}=0\{f, H\} = 0{f,H}=0. Canonical transformations are exactly the maps that preserve all brackets. Defined on the symplectic-form page.

Lie derivative

The rate of change of a T\tens{T}T along the θt\theta_tθt​ of a vector field X\tens{X}X:

£XT:=ddt∣t=0(θt∗T),\Lie_{\tens{X}} \tens{T} := \frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0} (\theta_t^* \tens{T}), £X​T:=dtd​​t=0​(θt∗​T),

Three different objects, one Italian mathematician. Context picks which is meant.

Minkowski space

The spacetime of special relativity: R4\mathbb{R}^4R4 with the global flat Lorentzian metric

η=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2\tens{\eta} = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 η=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2

(signature (−,+,+,+)(-, +, +, +)(−,+,+,+)). All Christoffel symbols vanish in these coordinates, so are straight lines and the Riemann tensor is zero — the “no gravity” special case that curved solutions approach asymptotically (Schwarzschild as r→∞r \to \inftyr→∞). Its group is the Poincaré group: translations plus Lorentz transformations. Every tangent space of a Lorentzian manifold is a copy of Minkowski space in miniature — the content of the Part I aside.

Compact support

A function (or vector field, or differential form) has compact support if it vanishes outside some compact subset K⊆MK \subseteq MK⊆M. On a non-compact manifold this is the condition that makes ∫M\int_M∫M​ converge and that kills the boundary contributions at infinity — it is why Stokes’s theorem and the integration of nnn-forms are stated for compactly supported forms. On a compact manifold every smooth function has compact support automatically, so the qualifier can be dropped.

Lie group

A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with multiplication and inversion smooth maps. Examples: GLn(R)GL_n(\mathbb{R})GLn​(R), the rotation groups SO(n)SO(n)SO(n), the Poincaré group of , Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn under addition, the circle S1S^1S1. The tangent space at the identity, with the bracket inherited from left-invariant vector fields, is the group’s . Isometry groups of pseudo-Riemannian manifolds are Lie groups — that is why counting counts a dimension.

Under a change of coordinates xμ↦x′μ′(x)x^\mu \mapsto x'^{\mu'}(x)xμ↦x′μ′(x), the components of an (r,s)(r, s)(r,s)-tensor transform as

T′μ1′⋯μr′ν1′⋯νs′=∂x′μ1′∂xμ1⋯∂x′μr′∂xμr  ∂xν1∂x′ν1′⋯∂xνs∂x′νs′  Tμ1⋯μrν1⋯νsT'^{\mu'_1 \cdots \mu'_r}{}_{\nu'_1 \cdots \nu'_s} = \frac{\partial x'^{\mu'_1}}{\partial x^{\mu_1}} \cdots \frac{\partial x'^{\mu'_r}}{\partial x^{\mu_r}}\; \frac{\partial x^{\nu_1}}{\partial x'^{\nu'_1}} \cdots \frac{\partial x^{\nu_s}}{\partial x'^{\nu'_s}}\; T^{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_r}{}_{\nu_1 \cdots \nu_s} T′μ1′​⋯μr′​ν1′​⋯νs′​​=∂xμ1​∂x′μ1′​​⋯∂xμr​∂x′μr′​​∂x′ν1′​∂xν1​​⋯∂x′νs′​∂xνs​​Tμ1​⋯μr​ν1​⋯νs​​

— one forward Jacobian factor per upper index, one inverse Jacobian factor per lower index. A component array obeying this rule on every chart overlap is a tensor; an array that picks up extra inhomogeneous terms (the Christoffel symbols are the standard example) is not. Stated and unpacked on the coordinate-components page.

Lovelock's theorem

In four dimensions, every symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor that is (i) built from the metric and at most its first and second derivatives and (ii) divergence-free is a linear combination

a Gμν+b gμνa\, G_{\mu\nu} + b\, g_{\mu\nu} aGμν​+bgμν​

of the Einstein tensor and the metric. So the left-hand side of the Einstein equations — including the cosmological-constant term — is forced, not chosen, once a tensorial second-order theory of the metric is demanded. In dimension n>4n > 4n>4, additional “Lovelock terms” (Gauss–Bonnet and higher) become available, which is one reason higher-dimensional gravity theories are less rigid than $4$D GR.

Embedded manifold

A smooth submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN is a subset M⊆RNM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NM⊆RN that is smoothly parametrized near each point: around every p∈Mp \in Mp∈M there is an open U⊆RNU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NU⊆RN, an open V⊆RnV \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nV⊆Rn, and a smooth map Φ:V→RN\Phi: V \to \mathbb{R}^NΦ:V→RN with everywhere-injective differential that is a homeomorphism onto U∩MU \cap MU∩M. The image Φ(V)\Phi(V)Φ(V) is an open piece of MMM, and the nnn coordinates on VVV are a chart on MMM.

The embedded view of differential geometry takes advantage of the ambient RN\mathbb{R}^NRN: tangent vectors are vectors in RN\mathbb{R}^NRN (spanning the tangent plane to MMM); the metric is the pullback of the Euclidean inner product; integration is over an embedded submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN. The Whitney embedding theorem says every smooth nnn-manifold can be embedded in R2n\mathbb{R}^{2n}R2n, so the embedded view loses no generality in principle. In practice the ambient space is excess baggage — isometric embeddings need many more dimensions (Nash), and a Lorentzian metric can only be induced from an indefinite-signature ambient space — which is why the abstract view is the working one.
